transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-18
Time: 16:00 UTC / 08:00 PT? (recording shows 16:00Z)
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connell (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Head of ML, Pioneer), Marco Ruiz (Platform Engineer), Sam Bennett (CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, i'm jordan from redwood, i'll keep it high level and priya will take us through optimize, the quant profiles and the bench flow.
[00:12] Aisha: thanks, jordan. quick context, we are evaluating ways to cut inference cost by ~30-50 while keeping our summarization quality within 2-3 points of our current baseline. we're using a 8k context model right now, mostly hosted on cloud gpus.
[00:25] Priya: great, that's exactly what optimize is designed for — we'll walk int8, fp8 profiles and show quality vs latency charts. quick ask before i dive in: marco, can you remind us of your typical qps and concurrency?
[00:38] Marco: sure, typical concurrency is 120 concurrent requests, peak bursts up to 400. avg tokens per request is around 150, but seq length varies a lot.
[00:47] Priya: perfect, that'll help with batching knobs. ok i'll share my screen — note, this is a pre-recorded demo environment so numbers are representative not exact.
[00:55] [01:05] Priya: first slide — quantization overview. INT8 gives the biggest cost reduction but can introduce quant noise for some layers, FP8 is a newer middle ground with lower degradation for decoder-style models. we use model-aware quant profiles so it's not a one-size-fits-all.
[01:30] Sam: can you explain model-aware? is it per-layer, or per-operator?
[01:36] Priya: it's per-layer and per-operator heuristics combined with a small calibration pass on a dev prompt set. basically we measure sensitivity and pick per-layer casting, sometimes keeping key layers in fp16 and others in int8.
[01:52] Aisha: we've had bad experiences where int8 collapsed outputs on summarization, is that still common?
[01:58] Priya: it's a risk; in our tests across 50+ models, raw int8 on some generator heads did reduce quality significantly. that's why optimize suggests mixed profiles: int8-heavy for MLP/attention matmuls that are robust, keep sensitive norm/LM heads higher precision or use fp8.
[02:20] [02:30] Jordan: justification point — customers often do a small eval on a held-out prompt set and check rouge/qa/semantic metrics. if delta is small they deploy int8, otherwise fp8 or mixed.
[02:42] Marco: how about latency? our SLOs are 200ms p95 for single-turn prompts. will int8 drop that below 200?
[02:52] Priya: typically int8 will reduce per-token latency by 20-40% depending on kernel support and sequence length; fp8 tends to be 10-25%. for your bursty pattern batching can help, but batching increases tail latency so we typically do continuous batching plus latency tiering.
[03:15] Priya: also we have kv cache prefix caching that reduces repeated context costs if you have many similar prompts, that can be a big win on cost and effective latency. sometimes the transcript labels it as k v cash in older transcribers ha.
[03:30] Aisha: interesting, we do a lot of docs summarization with repeated prefixes. that could help.
[03:35] [03:40] Liam: let me jump in with a screenshot — here's the optimize UI, you can see quant profile selector, quick quality-vs-latency chart for a sample model. notice the curve — int8 has a sharp drop in cost but a bit wider quality distribution.
[03:58] [04:05] Marco: is the quality-vs-latency plot driven by your internal evals or can we plug in our own prompts?
[04:12] Priya: you can upload your prompt set and run a benchmark. that's how we recommend doing pilots. the UI supports CSV prompts and ground truth labels for rouge/accuracy so you get direct deltas.
[04:26] Sam: for the pilot, will you run the bench in our VPC or on hosted infra?
[04:33] Jordan: usually for proofs we run first on hosted to iterate fast; once you're comfortable we can run the Dedicated pilot or private deployment in your VPC. for security we have SOC2, SSO and KMS integrations — we'll share the docs.
[04:48] Aisha: ok send SOC2 and KMS details. encryption at rest with customer KMS is required for us.
[04:54] Jordan: noted, i'll attach that after the call.
[05:00] [05:10] Priya: back to bench methodology: we'll run INT8, FP8, mixed, and baseline fp16. we capture token-level latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), cost per 1k tokens, and quality metrics and then produce a delta table.
[05:26] Priya: one nuance — for very long sequences fp8 sometimes wins on latency because of kernel packing and reduced memory bandwidth pressure. for short sequences int8 often has the best cost numbers.
[05:40] Marco: what's the expected turnaround for a bench run on our 2k prompt set?
[05:46] Priya: depends on concurrency and tokens but for a 2k set we usually get results within 24-48 hours on hosted clusters; on Dedicated it'd be faster if we reserve capacity.
[05:58] Sam: pricing question — Dedicated reserved capacity, how flexible? we're not ready for a year commitment.
[06:05] Jordan: we offer 3-month pilot reserved pools with month-to-month roll options. I'll include the pricing sheet.
[06:12] [06:18] Aisha: any differences in observability between hosted and dedicated? we need token-level cost breakdowns and model routes traces.
[06:26] Liam: observability is the same interface; Dedicated gives you private metrics retention options and longer retention windows as an add-on. traces and per-route dashboards are identical.
[06:36] Marco: we use SAML SSO and have strict RBAC, do you support SCIM?
[06:42] Jordan: yes SAML and SCIM provisioning supported, and we can map roles to RBAC in the console.
[06:49] [06:52] Priya: quick demo clip — here's a bench result for a customer similar to you: 2.5x cost reduction on INT8 with a 3% rouge drop; FP8 yielded 1.8x cost reduction with 1% rouge drop. the latency p95 dropped from 420ms to 280ms in INT8 for their workload.
[07:13] Aisha: those numbers are promising but i need to see our exact metrics.
[07:18] Priya: understood, that's why we run your prompts. also we'll include human-sampled quality checks and an explanation of failure modes.
[07:28] [07:35] Marco: on model variants — if we pin a version and it regresses after quantization changes, how do rollouts work?
[07:43] Liam: we support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies: you can route a small percentage to the quantized variant and monitor metrics; if quality drops beyond thresholds we auto-fallback to baseline.
[07:58] Sam: good, rollback automation is critical.
[08:02] [08:10] Aisha: latency SLOs again — can we specify per-route SLOs so critical routes stay on fp16 or fp8 and cheap routes use int8?
[08:18] Priya: yes, per-route model and quant profile assignment is supported; Optimize recommends defaults but you can pin per-route.
[08:26] [08:30] Jordan: quick note on costs — the platform shows unit economics and you can simulate savings at scale based on your qps and token distribution.
[08:40] Marco: any gotchas with transformer variants? we've got a custom decoder-only model that diverges slightly from open checkpoints.
[08:48] Priya: custom models require a short onboarding: a calibration pass and a smoke bench; sometimes we need to keep specific layers at higher precision. it's part of the pilot scope.
[08:58] [09:05] Aisha: ok what's the timeline if we sign up for a 3-month pilot?
[09:09] Jordan: we can start the bench within 3 business days after you share the prompt set and credentials for a hosted run; Dedicated pilot provisioning usually takes 7-10 days depending on capacity.
[09:20] Aisha: we'll aim to share prompts by end of week.
[09:24] Jordan: great. summary of next steps — jordan will send SOC2/KMS/SSO docs and pricing, priya will schedule bench and run INT8/FP8 on your 2k set, marco will send the prompt set and concurrency numbers.
[09:38] [09:45] Sam: one last thing, any competitors that do this better? we evaluated replicate but their dedicated tooling lacked enterprise RBAC.
[09:53] Jordan: Replicate is more developer-focused but gaps around enterprise controls and observability are common. we'll share a short competitor matrix.
[10:02] Aisha: thanks everyone, this was helpful. looking forward to the bench.
[10:06] Jordan: thanks — we'll follow up with notes and the deck.

Meeting end

Notes on transcription: occasional word swaps (k v cache as k v cash), some names may be mis-labeled in raw transcript exports, timestamps approximate.
